title: GitLab Flow
description: Combine feature branching with environment-based promotion in the GitLab Flow model.

data.text: GitLab Flow extends GitHub Flow with environment-based branches. Instead of merging to main and deploying immediately, you promote code through environment branches (staging, pre-production, production) using merge requests. This gives you control over when and where code is deployed.
In the environment-based model, feature branches merge into a staging branch. When staging is stable, staging is merged into production. Each environment has its own branch and CI/CD pipeline.

data.title: GitLab Flow with environment branches
data.code:
# Feature branch: develop and test locally
git switch -c feature/search-filters
# ... commits ...
git push origin feature/search-filters

# Merge to staging via merge request
git switch staging
git merge --no-ff feature/search-filters
# CI deploys to staging environment

# After QA approval, promote to production
git switch production
git merge --no-ff staging
# CI deploys to production

data.text: For projects with explicit versions, GitLab Flow uses a master branch plus per-release branches. The master branch always reflects the latest stable release. Features merge into master; release branches branch from master for version-specific maintenance.

items: **feature/** — Branched from master for new work
**Merge request** — The integration point with review and CI

data.title: GitLab Flow is not GitLab-specific
data.text: You can implement the GitLab Flow model with GitHub, Bitbucket, or any Git platform that supports environment branches and merge requests.

Merge requests in GitLab Flow serve as the primary quality gate. They support code review, automated testing, security scanning, and approval workflows. Only code that passes all checks should be promoted to the next environment.

data.title: Configure branch protection in GitLab
data.code:
# .gitlab/merge_request_templates/default.md
## Merge Request Checklist

- [ ] CI pipeline passes
- [ ] Unit tests pass
- [ ] Code reviewed by at least 1 teammate
- [ ] Security scan shows no new vulnerabilities
- [ ] QA verified in staging environment

## Environment Promotion

- [ ] Staging deploy verified
- [ ] Product owner approved for production

cards.title: vs GitHub Flow
cards.description: GitLab Flow adds environment branches, giving more control over deployment timing. GitHub Flow deploys every merge to main.

cards.title: vs Git Flow
cards.description: GitLab Flow is simpler — no develop branch, no release branches. It uses environment branches instead of formal release lifecycle.

cards.title: vs trunk-based
cards.description: GitLab Flow allows slightly longer-lived branches (per-environment). Trunk-based encourages all work on main.

items.question: How many environment branches do I need?
items.answer: At minimum, production and staging. Add pre-production, QA, or feature-preview branches as needed by your release process.

items.question: What happens when staging and production diverge?
items.answer: Fix the divergence immediately. If a hotfix went to production without passing through staging, cherry-pick or merge it to staging to realign.

items.question: Can I use GitLab Flow with feature flags?
items.answer: Yes. Feature flags complement environment branches by letting you deploy incomplete features to staging without exposing them to production users.

items.question: Do I need a separate GitLab instance?
items.answer: No. You can use GitLab.com (SaaS) or self-host GitLab. The flow is independent of the hosting choice.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: GitLab Flow uses environment branches to control deployment promotion
Feature branches merge into staging; staging promotes to production
Merge requests serve as quality gates with review and CI
Simpler than Git Flow with more deployment control than GitHub Flow
Applicable on any Git platform that supports branch-based pipelines
